claims.proposition: A lithium-ion cell that rests at a high state of charge stores more entropic heat than the same cell at a low state of charge.
A lithium-ion cell whose internal resistance rises with age generates more heat at the same discharge current.
Electrochemical reactions inside a lithium-ion cell convert chemical energy into electrical work and release the remainder as heat.
Joule heating in the electrolyte of a lithium-ion cell accounts for a small share of the total heat generated under a high discharge rate.
Tabulated heat generation curves for a lithium-ion cell are usually measured at a constant temperature and a constant current.
The adiabatic temperature rise of a lithium-ion cell during a high-rate discharge is proportional to the energy released and inversely proportional to the heat capacity of the cell.
The entropic heat of a lithium-ion cell changes sign when the cell voltage crosses the entropic coefficient of its chemistry.
The heat generated during a fast charge of a lithium-ion cell is concentrated near the electrode surface where the reaction front advances.
The heat generation rate of a lithium-ion cell at a given current does not depend on the capacity of the cell in ampere hours.
The irreversible heat source of a lithium-ion cell grows with the square of the current drawn from it.
The onset of thermal runaway in a lithium-ion cell is preceded by a rise of the internal gas pressure inside the sealed enclosure.
Thermal runaway in a lithium-ion cell begins with a localised rise of temperature and does not occur while the ambient temperature stays below the melting point of the separator.
A cold plate bonded to the base of a prismatic cell removes heat by conducting it into a circulating coolant.
A cooling plate with a serpentine channel supports a uniform coolant velocity across the whole footprint of the cell.
A heat pipe that links a cell to a radiator uses the latent heat of a working fluid to transport energy across the gap.
A liquid cooling loop that pumps an aqueous glycol mixture controls the maximum temperature of the cells it serves.
A pack that uses air cooling relies on the natural convection of ambient air across fins attached to the cells.
A passive spreader plate transports the heat of a cell across a larger surface before the coolant reaches it.
An immersion cooling bath contains the cell completely and transfers heat by convection at the wetted surface.
The coolant flow rate through a cold plate determines how much heat the plate carries away from the cell.
The pumping power of a liquid cooling loop grows with the square of the coolant velocity inside the tubing.
The thermal design of a pack determines the maximum sustained discharge current of every cell inside it.
The thermal interface material between a cell and its cold plate determines the temperature difference across the joint.
The time constant of a cooling loop describes how quickly the coolant temperature approaches the cell temperature.
A lithium-ion cell that is kept at a high storage temperature ages faster than the same cell kept at room temperature.
A lithium-ion cell that is stored fully charged for a long period loses more capacity than the same cell stored at a middle state of charge.
A lithium-ion cell whose electrodes have lost contact with their current collector shows a sudden rise of the internal resistance.
Anode plating of lithium metal reduces the usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell charged at a low temperature.
Calendar ageing of a lithium-ion cell occurs even when the cell is not being discharged.
Repeated cycling of a lithium-ion cell produces a slow loss of the available capacity of the cell.
The capacity fade of a lithium-ion cell depends on the depth of the discharge cycles it undergoes.
The end of the service life of a lithium-ion cell is usually defined by a loss of a fixed share of the original capacity.
The gas produced by side reactions in a lithium-ion cell swells the pouch of a prismatic cell.
The growth of the solid electrolyte layer on the anode of a lithium-ion cell uses part of the lithium inventory of the cell.
The impedance of a lithium-ion cell rises as the electrodes become coated with the products of side reactions.
The resistance of the electrolyte of a lithium-ion cell grows as the salt concentration of the electrolyte falls during an extended discharge.
A barcode reader provides the identity of the specimen that a technician loads into the test bench.
A calorimeter measures the total energy a laboratory cell releases during a complete discharge.
A data logger samples the sensor channels of a test bench at a fixed rate and stores them on a local disk.
A fume hood captures the gaseous products released by a cell that vents during an abuse test.
A humidity sensor installed in a test chamber observes the moisture of the air around the cell.
A potentiostat provides a controlled current to a laboratory cell and measures its terminal voltage.
A reference electrode placed next to a half cell measures the potential of the working electrode directly.
A reference thermometer placed in the coolant stream measures the temperature the loop actually carries.
A thermocouple glued to the surface of a cell measures the external temperature of the cell.
A vibration shaker produces the mechanical excitation that a vehicle delivers to a battery pack.
An environmental chamber controls the air temperature and the relative humidity around the specimen.
An ultrasonic probe reveals the delamination of the electrode stack of a prismatic cell.
A salt marsh that receives freshwater inflow causes more organic carbon to accumulate in its sediment.
Compaction of marsh sediment increases with depth and reduces the space available for further burial.
Mineral sediment that buries marsh soil reduces the oxidation of the buried organic carbon.
Organic carbon that leaves a marsh in surface water is exported rather than buried.
Salt-marsh sediment stores organic carbon from the water column as particles settle onto the marsh surface.
Sediment accretion on a salt marsh increases the elevation of the surface relative to the surrounding water.
Sulfate reduction in marsh sediment produces sulfide that binds iron and slows the release of buried carbon.
The accumulation rate of organic carbon in salt-marsh sediment depends on the supply of fine particles from the estuary.
The burial depth of a salt-marsh soil column determines how long the buried carbon stays away from the air.
The carbon content of salt-marsh sediment decreases with depth as the oldest material decomposes.
The rate of decomposition of buried marsh organic carbon increases when the water table falls.
The residence time of organic carbon in marsh sediment is measured in centuries rather than in years.
A microbial community below the oxic surface of marsh sediment converts the organic matter more slowly than one at the surface.
A productive marsh supports its microbial community with more organic substrate.
Anaerobic microbes in marsh sediment use sulfate instead of oxygen when the soil is saturated.
Bacterial sulphate reduction in a salt marsh is faster in the warm season than in the cold season.
Enzyme activity in marsh soil decreases sharply when the soil dries out.
Iron reduction in marsh sediment competes with methanogenesis for the hydrogen that fermentation supplies.
Microbial respiration in marsh soil converts organic carbon into carbon dioxide that escapes to the atmosphere.
The ammonium that marsh microbes release feeds the primary production of marsh plants.
The methanogenic community of a salt marsh produces methane from the acetate that fermentation releases.
The microbial turnover of marsh organic matter controls how much carbon the marsh releases as carbon dioxide.
The rate of microbial respiration in marsh soil depends on the temperature of the soil and on its moisture.
The respiration rate of a marsh soil sample changes within hours of the sample being brought into the laboratory.
A levee that isolates a marsh from the floodplain reduces the supply of the river sediment the marsh needs.
A marsh that loses its creek network reduces the exchange of water and sediment with the estuary.
A restored marsh in front of a seawall dissipates wave energy and reduces the erosion of the shoreline.
A seawall without a marsh in front of it reflects the incoming wave energy back onto the shore.
A storm surge causes new sediment to be transported onto the surface of a low marsh.
Dredging of a navigation channel increases the tidal prism and deepens the water beside the marsh.
Erosion of the shoreline of a coastal plain removes the sediment that the marsh needs to accrete.
Relative sea level rise drowns the marsh platform where the sediment supply cannot keep pace.
The landward migration of a marsh requires space that is free of fixed structures.
The rate of marsh loss along a developed shoreline is higher than the rate of marsh gain on a sheltered one.
The width of the marsh belt is the main factor that controls how much wave energy reaches the shoreline.
Vegetation loss on a marsh platform increases the exposure of the soil to wave erosion.
A chamber built around a patch of marsh soil measures the carbon dioxide that escapes from it.
A dissolved carbon analyser measures the concentration of carbon compounds in the sampled water.
A drone moves along a survey line above the marsh and photographs the creek network from above.
A field notebook notes the date, the time and the weather of every measurement round.
A flux tower measures the wind speed above the marsh canopy.
A gas chromatograph separates the methane and the carbon dioxide of a gas sample.
A laboratory balance measures the sediment samples that the core cutter brought up.
A piezometer measures the depth of the water table inside the marsh soil.
A sediment core shows the vertical sequence of deposits in a marsh soil column.
A trap stores the material that the incoming tide brings onto the marsh surface.
A water sampler takes a known volume of water from the creek that drains the marsh.
An echosounder shows the elevation of the marsh surface along a transect.
